ety.text: Exact origin unknown. The earliest recorded reference for the noun was to heavy, useless objects such as old, discarded furniture. Perhaps from the verb lumber in reference to meaning "awkward to move"; Online Etymological Dictionary thinks this may derive from the same root as lame. Possibly influenced by Lumbar, an obsolete variant of Lombard, the Italian immigrant class known for being pawnbrokers and money-lenders in early England. Compare English lumpish.

senses.d: Wood sawn into planks or otherwise prepared for sale or use, especially as a building material.
Old furniture or other items that take up room, or are stored away.
Useless or cumbrous material.
ex: The bookful blockhead ignorantly read, / With loads of learned lumber in his head,[…]

senses.d: A pawnbroker's shop, or room for storing articles put in pawn; hence, a pledge, or pawn.
A baseball bat.
An erect penis.
To move clumsily and heavily; to move slowly.
To load down with things, to fill, to encumber, to impose an unwanted burden on.
ex: They’ve lumbered me with all these suitcases.
I got lumbered with that boring woman all afternoon.

senses.d: To heap together in disorder.
To fill or encumber with lumber.
To pawn (goods).

ety.text: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin lignāmen. Compare Sicilian lignami.

From Middle English lumpe, from a Germanic base akin to Proto-Germanic *limpaną (“to glide, go, hang loosely”). Compare Dutch lomp (“rag”), German Low German Lump (“rag”), German Lumpen (“rag”) and Lump (“ragamuffin”).

senses.d: Something that protrudes, sticks out, or sticks together; a cluster or blob; a mound or mass of no particular shape.
ex: Stir the gravy until there are no more lumps.
a lump of coal; a lump of clay; a lump of cheese

senses.d: A swelling or nodule of tissue under the skin or in an internal part of the body.
ex: Lumps in the breasts are an indicator of breast cancer.

senses.d: A group, set, or unit.
ex: The money arrived all at once as one big lump sum payment.

senses.d: A small, shaped mass of sugar, typically about a teaspoonful.
ex: Do you want one lump or two with your coffee?

senses.d: A dull or lazy person.
ex: Don't just sit there like a lump.
"Thou great Norman lump!" he muttered. "If I conjure till Doomsday, I cannot make thee gold."

senses.d: A fat person.
A beating or verbal abuse.
ex: He's taken his lumps over the years.
Komer admitted that the United States would probably suffer "short term lumps" as a result of Johnson's brusque decision.

senses.d: A projection beneath the breech end of a gun barrel.
A kind of fish, the lumpsucker.
ex: You roast him [the fish] […] just like a lump.

senses.d: Food given to a tramp to be eaten on the road.
To treat as a single unit; to group together in a casual or chaotic manner (as if forming an ill-defined lump of the items).
ex: People tend to lump turtles and tortoises together, when in fact they are different creatures.
Most gays don't want to know about us, so lumping us in their support efforts is counter-productive at best.

senses.d: To bear (a heavy or awkward burden); to carry (something unwieldy) from one place to another.
To burden (someone) with an undesired task or responsibility.
To hit or strike (a person).
ex: If that's the only way you can fight, then you'd better be prepared to get lumped.

senses.d: To form a lump or lumps.
ex: Thin the paint with mineral spirits for a medium consistency so that it will not drip or lump.
